items.stem: The main consequence of near multicollinearity is:
items.explanation: Near dependence can inflate coefficient variances and standard errors; it does not by itself create bias.

items.stem: Perfect multicollinearity means:
options: Exact linear dependence among columns of X
items.explanation: Perfect collinearity is exact linear dependence, so X loses column rank.

items.stem: If X has perfect multicollinearity, then X′X is:
items.explanation: Exact column dependence makes X′X singular.

items.stem: Does multicollinearity alone bias OLS when E(u|X)=0 holds?
items.explanation: Exogeneity gives OLS unbiasedness; collinearity affects precision.

items.stem: If an auxiliary regression has R²ⱼ=0.80, calculate VIFⱼ.
An estimate is 3 and its standard error is 1.5. What is the t statistic for H₀:β=0?
Which pattern is a common warning sign of multicollinearity?
options: Low R² and all coefficients highly significant
High R² with weak individual t statistics
A zero residual sum of squares
items.explanation: Strong joint fit can coexist with imprecise individual coefficients.

items.stem: The VIF for predictor j is:
items.explanation: VIF is the reciprocal of one minus the auxiliary-regression R².

items.stem: Which statement about coefficient magnitude is correct?
options: Multicollinearity always makes estimates close to zero
Magnitude is not a necessary consequence; imprecision is the general concern
items.explanation: The robust general consequence is inflated variance, not a guaranteed direction or size of the point estimate.

items.stem: Pairwise correlations may fail to detect multicollinearity because:
options: A predictor can be explained by a combination of several other predictors
They depend on the response variable
They are always zero in multiple regression
items.explanation: An auxiliary regression can reveal joint dependence not visible in any single pairwise correlation.

items.stem: Which statements are correct? A. Near multicollinearity can inflate standard errors. B. It automatically biases OLS. C. R² can remain high. D. Individual t statistics can be weak.
items.explanation: A, C and D are true. Collinearity alone does not create bias under exogeneity.
statements: Near multicollinearity can inflate standard errors.
Individual t statistics can be weak.

A.why: The variance of affected coefficient estimators can rise.

B.why: Collinearity alone does not violate exogeneity.

D.why: Large standard errors can weaken t statistics.

items.stem: If R²ⱼ=0.90, calculate VIFⱼ.
If a standard error increases from 0.5 to 2 while the estimate stays fixed, by what factor does its variance increase?
items.explanation: Variance is SE². The ratio is 2²/0.5²=4/0.25=16.

items.stem: Which statements distinguish perfect from near multicollinearity? A. Perfect collinearity is exact dependence. B. Near collinearity can retain full rank. C. Perfect collinearity makes X′X singular. D. Near collinearity always makes OLS biased.
items.explanation: A, B and C are true; D is false because collinearity alone does not cause bias under exogeneity.

items.stem: If β̂=2.4 and SE=1.2, calculate |t| for testing β=0.
Which is a possible consequence of deleting a relevant predictor correlated with included regressors?
items.explanation: Omitting a relevant correlated variable can make the composite error correlated with included regressors.

items.stem: Which is NOT generally a consequence of near multicollinearity under exogeneity?
options: Unstable estimates under small data changes
Weak individual significance despite high R²
items.explanation: The expected value of OLS remains correct under exogeneity; multicollinearity affects precision.

Which statements about remedies are defensible? A. Collecting more informative data may help. B. Dropping any correlated predictor is always harmless. C. Ridge regression can stabilise prediction while introducing shrinkage bias. D. Principal components can replace correlated variables with orthogonal combinations.
items.explanation: A, C and D are defensible. Dropping a relevant correlated variable may create omitted-variable bias.
